canvas-06.description: Printed sheet 6 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch and scanned from another copy on cream paper, covers the commercial centre of the borough east of the railroad. The sheet is turned on the page so that Main runs down the right-hand side and Fairmount Avenue crosses the top. The curved tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad sweep from the upper centre to the lower left, passing the Lackawanna freight house and a yard of sidings, and a station building stands where the line meets Railroad Avenue. Passaic Avenue, also lettered Railroad Avenue, runs along the tracks and carries the main street frontage of stores, a laundry, a restaurant, a tailor, the post office and the Fairview Garage, with the club house of the Chatham Fish and Game Protective Association and the Chatham Public Library near the top. West of the railroad lie blocks of frame dwellings between Second Street, Maple Avenue, Dempster and Hillside Avenue, including J. R. Littlejohn's greenhouses. Fuller Avenue, also lettered Bowers Lane, crosses the middle. South of Hillside Avenue the blocks 37, 36 and 33 front Summit Avenue and New Avenue, and open land fills the large block 123 between Myrtle Avenue, Fern Avenue and Minton Avenue. In the lower left corner E. P. Miller's coal yard, a vacant building and a bridge over the Passaic River mark the city limits of Summit. Water pipes, hydrants and house numbers are marked along the streets. The compass, scale bar and title cartouche are drawn on the sheet and the adjoining sheets 4, 5, 8, 9 and 10 are named at the edges.
notes: Canvas canvas-06 is printed sheet 6, a scan of another copy on cream paper.
Railroad Avenue and New Avenue are not in today's street network under these names; Passaic Avenue here is South Passaic Avenue east of the railroad in OpenStreetMap and Dempster is Dempster Road.

Minton Avenue / Main Street, Minton Avenue / Myrtle Avenue and Minton Avenue / Vine Street fitted 5 to 7 m off against the rest of the part and the Minton Avenue junctions were left out; Myrtle Avenue / Summit Avenue (the junction with New Avenue, 5 m residual and about 15 m from the drawn corner) and the duplicate Hillside Avenue / Main Street node were also left out.
2nd Street / Fairmount Avenue is 5 m off in this part and was left out.
Lackawanna Freight House, E. P. Miller's coal yard and the Fairview Garage are on this sheet.

Printed sheet 6, 100 ft (scan of another copy, cream paper). Downtown east: Main Street, Passaic Avenue, Railroad Avenue, Summit Avenue, the D.L.&W. station. Minton Avenue junctions (5-7 m), Myrtle / Summit and 2nd Street / Fairmount left out.

canvas-09.description: Sheet 7 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the north-western corner of the borough between Main Street, which runs down the left edge of the sheet, and the open land to the east. The sheet is turned so that north points to the upper right. Brook Lake Road runs along the top as the borough line with Madison, whose water works hydrant stands at the corner of Division Avenue and Main Street; the margin refers to the borough map of Madison. Below it the only built-up streets are Garden Avenue and the short Garden Place, lined with narrow lots and a few frame dwellings, poultry houses and auto houses, and a row of dwellings on Main Street. Most of the sheet is the large blocks 107 and 108. Block 108 holds the greenhouses of Antonio Ruszika, a group of long glass houses with sheds, and near Black Brook the Chatham Water and Light Station, with its pumps, boilers and dynamos listed beside it. Block 107 holds the greenhouses of Robert Roper at the upper right. Black Brook winds across the lower part of the sheet and passes under Main Street in a culvert next to the junction with Lafayette Avenue at the bottom left, where a lane also leaves Main Street. Water pipes of 4 and 10 inches and hydrants are marked along Main Street and Garden Avenue. The sheet numbers 1, 2, 4 and 8 mark the adjoining sheets.
notes: This canvas is a scan of a second copy of the atlas; canvas sheet-6 is a damaged scan of the same printed sheet 7 and was not used.
Brook Lake Road is spelled Brooklake Road today.

Only four junctions are usable (three on Main Street and Garden Avenue / Garden Place); Lafayette Avenue / Main Street was hand-picked. The fitted scale is about 4 percent below the other 100 ft sheets.
The Ruszika and Roper greenhouses and the Chatham Water and Light Station are on this sheet.

Printed sheet 7, 100 ft (scan of another copy). North-west: Main Street, Brook Lake Road (Madison line), Garden Avenue, Garden Place; Ruszika greenhouses, Chatham Water and Light Station on Black Brook; mostly open land.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the western end of the borough along the Madison line. The sheet is turned on the page so that Main Street runs down the right-hand edge and Lafayette Avenue crosses the bottom. A Borough Line is drawn along the top, with the lettering See Borough Map of Madison, and a second line cuts diagonally across the upper left to separate Chatham Borough from Chatham Township. Most of the sheet is open land. Woodland Road runs from the top to Lafayette Avenue as a long, wide, undeveloped strip, with the tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad beside it, running through block 114 and crossing Lafayette Avenue at the bottom. Kings Road leaves the top near Division Avenue and bends south-east to meet Lafayette Avenue a short way west of Main Street. Between Kings Road and Main Street lies a strip of narrow house lots, with frame dwellings, coops, sheds, a cabinet maker's shop and garages scattered along the Main Street front, and an abandoned right of way of the D.L. and W. R.R. cuts the block diagonally; at the top Hedges Avenue is shown as not open. A brook with a culvert crosses beneath Main Street near Lafayette Avenue, and water pipes of 4 and 10 inches are marked. The compass, scale bar, the Nov. 1921 Chatham title cartouche and the sheet number 2 are in the margins. Adjoining sheets are numbered 12, 4 and 7.
notes: Canvas sheet-2 is printed sheet 2.
Brooklake Road / Division Avenue / Main Street lies at the very top edge of the sheet and was left out.
The railroad is lettered D.L. & W. R.R.; the right of way beside Kings Road is lettered Abandoned Right of Way.

Woodland Road meets Lafayette Avenue about 30 m from the modern junction (also on sheet 4), Main Street / Lafayette Avenue and Kings Road / Lafayette Avenue as detected disagree by 8 to 30 m; the part is placed from Garden Avenue / Main Street (hand-picked), Kings Road / Lafayette Avenue (carried from sheet 4) and Division Avenue / Kings Road at the top edge.

Printed sheet 2, 100 ft. West end along the Madison line: Main Street, Kings Road, Woodland Road, Lafayette Avenue, D.L.&W. railroad; mostly open land. Placed from three points: Garden Avenue / Main Street (hand-picked), Kings Road / Lafayette Avenue (carried from sheet-4), Division Avenue / Kings Road (detected at the top edge). Woodland Road / Lafayette Avenue is about 30 m off its modern node and is not used.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the south-western part of the borough around the crossing of Washington Avenue and Watchung Avenue. The sheet is turned on the page, so the streets run across it at an angle rather than square to its edges. Lafayette Avenue crosses the top right, Washington Avenue runs across the middle, and Fairmount Avenue crosses the bottom, with Watchung Avenue, Orchard Road, Oliver and Chatham as cross streets from left to right. The north-western half is largely open or sparsely built land: W. G. Badgely's greenhouses stand between Watchung Avenue and Lafayette Avenue, and the large blocks 132 and 133 and the land west of Watchung Avenue hold only a few dwellings, coops and sheds. Between Watchung Avenue and Chatham, north of Washington Avenue, are blocks 131, 31 1/2 and 31 cut into narrow lots, with a street lettered Not Opened between Watchung Avenue and Orchard Road and a Lincoln Avenue block beside Lafayette Avenue. South of Washington Avenue the lots are mostly built with frame dwellings. St. Patrick's R.C. Church, its school, convent and priest's house occupy block 32 beside Chatham, and the Congregational church stands at the south end of Orchard Road. Block 11 to the south-west holds scattered dwellings, a gasoline tank and garages. Lumm Avenue crosses the lower right. Water pipes of 4, 6 and 10 inches, hydrants and house numbers are marked along the streets. The sheet number 3, the Nov. 1921 title cartouche, a compass and a scale bar are drawn in the margins, and the adjoining sheets 12, 4 and 5 are named at the edges.
notes: Canvas sheet-3 is printed sheet 3.
Lumm Avenue is Lum Avenue today.
Ascension Place and Brook Street are not in today's street network; the street lettered Lane at the top left is not in the modern network under that name.
Lincoln Avenue is drawn about 9 m from the modern street (Lincoln / Chatham Street 8.7 m off in a trial fit) and was left out of the fit.
Chatham Street / Lum Avenue and the Lafayette Avenue junctions at the top were not detected; the part is placed from eight junctions along Washington Avenue, Fairmount Avenue and the cross streets.
St. Patrick's R.C. Church, School, Convent and Priest's House, W. G. Badgely's greenhouses and a Congregational church are on this sheet.
Printed sheet 3, 100 ft. South-west of downtown: Lafayette, Washington, Watchung, Fairmount and Lincoln Avenues. Lincoln Avenue displaced about 9 m, left out.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the western side of the borough's centre between Chatham Street on the west and Main Street on the east, from La Fayette Avenue at the top of the sheet to Fairmount Avenue at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page so that north points to the upper right. The tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad cross the sheet from top to bottom, with Front Street along their west side and two station buildings beside them. West of the railroad the blocks between Lincoln Avenue, Washington Avenue and Lumm Avenue are laid out in narrow house lots with frame dwellings, poultry houses and sheds, and the long glass houses of the Chatham Rose Company occupy the block south of Washington Avenue and a strip beside Front Street. The large block between Lumm Avenue and Fairmount Avenue is mostly open land, with Chatham Public School No. 1 and its detached classrooms near Fairmount Avenue. East of the railroad, between the tracks and Main Street, are dwellings and stores on the street front, Bond Street, the Borough Hall and the fire department with its auto truck. Smaller streets named on the sheet include Maple, Brook and Walnut between Lincoln and Washington Avenues, Ward Place and Elmwood Avenue off Main Street, Center Street at the bottom right, Second Street and Maple Avenue south of Fairmount Avenue, Woodland Road and Kings Road at the top. Water pipe sizes, hydrants and house numbers are marked along the streets. The edges of sheets 2, 3, 6, 7 and 8 adjoin on the margins.
notes: Maple (between Lincoln and Washington Avenues) is today's Cherry Lane.
Lumm Avenue is spelled Lum Avenue today.
Brook (between Chatham Street and Maple) and Bond (off Main Street) are not in today's street network.
Lincoln Avenue east of Chatham Street is drawn about 9 m south of the modern street; its junctions were left out of the fit.
The west ends of La Fayette Avenue and Fairmount Avenue (at Chatham Street and Second Street) disagree with the modern streets by 6 to 9 m and were left out of the fit.
The Chatham Rose Company greenhouses, Chatham Public School No. 1, the Borough Hall and fire department, and the railroad station are on this sheet.

Printed sheet 4, 100 ft. Downtown west: Main Street, Washington, Lincoln, Fairmount Avenues, the railroad; pilot sheet. Lincoln Avenue (about 9 m off), Chatham / Lafayette, Chatham / Fairmount and 2nd / Fairmount left out.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the south-eastern part of the borough between Fairmount Avenue at the top and the Passaic River at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page, so Watchung Avenue runs from the top centre down to the lower left corner and Hillside Avenue crosses the middle. Along Fairmount Avenue the street front is lined with frame dwellings, with Orchard Road, Oliver Street and Chatham Street entering from sheet 3 at the top, and Ascension Place at the top left. Between Fairmount Avenue and Hillside Avenue the large block 8 holds the glass houses of Frank L. Moope, florist, whose Sunnywood Greenhouses stand behind Fuller Avenue, also lettered Bower Lane, with house lots along Maple Avenue at the right edge. West of Watchung Avenue the blocks 136 and 137 lie between Ascension Place, Edgehill Avenue and Charles Place. South of Hillside Avenue are blocks 134, 40 and 39, with Overlook and Raymond as cross streets, and D. Falconer, florist, has long greenhouses at Raymond. Bridge Street, Girard Avenue and an auto repair shop stand above the tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad, which cross the lower part of the sheet from left to right. Below the railroad, block 135 is open ground running to the Passaic River, drawn along the lower right with the Passaic City Line marked in it and the legend See Map of Summit. River Road meets Watchung Avenue at the bottom left. Hydrants, water pipes of 4, 6 and 10 inches and house numbers are marked.
notes: Canvas sheet-5 is printed sheet 5.
Fuller Avenue (Bower Lane), Maple Avenue, Raymond and Ascension Place are not in today's street network under these names; Overlook is Overlook Road and Raymond is Raymond Street in OpenStreetMap.
Chatham Street / Fairmount Avenue was 10 m from the fit and was rejected; Edgehill Avenue / Watchung Avenue is 5 m off.
The Passaic River and the Summit city line form the south-east edge; the margin reads See Map of Summit.
Printed sheet 5, 100 ft. South-east: Fairmount and Hillside Avenues, Bridge Street, Edgehill Avenue, Charles Place, railroad, Passaic River (see map of Summit).

sheet-7.description: Printed sheet 8 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the area north of the centre of the borough between Main, which runs down the left edge, and Weston Avenue near the right edge at the bottom. The sheet is turned on the page, so Main Street appears as a long street running down the left side with a bend at the top, and Passaic Avenue crosses the bottom. The upper two thirds is mostly open land. A strip of lots along Main Street from Washington Avenue to Ward Place holds frame dwellings, with Ward Place and a second Ward Pl. turning off it, and a lane at the top is shown as a dashed outline; Black Brook crosses the top edge. In the middle of the sheet the large block 27 is nearly empty, with a few farm buildings, sheds and poultry houses. Elmwood Avenue runs across the lower part from Main Street towards the right edge, with the Ogden Memorial Presbyterian Church at its west end, steam heated and electric lighted, and small dwellings and poultry houses on both sides. Between Elmwood Avenue and Passaic Avenue, the Center streets and lots of block 1 and block 2 are laid out. Near Main Street the frontage has stores, a bank, an undertaker, and the M.E. Church, with Center Avenue and Center forming the street pattern leading to Weston Avenue. Block 33 at the bottom right is divided into many long empty lots. Fairmount Avenue meets Main Street at the left. Water pipes, hydrants and house numbers are marked. Sheets 4, 6, 7 and 9 adjoin on the margins, and the Nov. 1921 title, compass and scale bar are on the sheet.
notes: Canvas sheet-7 is printed sheet 8.
Center is today's Center Street / Center Place, and Passaic Avenue is North Passaic Avenue in OpenStreetMap.

Ward Place here does not follow the modern Ward Place, which curves differently; Main Street / Ward Place and Main Street / Washington Avenue were not detected and the part is placed from junctions between Elmwood Avenue and Passaic Avenue.
The lettering of Fairmount Avenue at the left edge is partly hidden by water-pipe lines and reads Fairmoun Av. in places.
Bond Street is not in today's street network.
Printed sheet 8, 100 ft. North of Main Street: Center Avenue, Elmwood Avenue; Ogden Memorial Church. Ward Place not drawn like the modern street.

sheet-8.description: Printed sheet 9 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the north-eastern part of the borough between Main, which runs down the left side, and Weston Avenue and Florham Road along the right. The sheet is turned on the page, so the streets cross it nearly horizontally: Passaic Avenue along the top, then North Hillside Avenue, North Summit Avenue and Hedges Avenue in turn, all running east from Main towards Weston Avenue. The blocks between them, numbered 3, 34, 112 and 35, are cut into narrow deep lots, most of them with a single frame dwelling, garage or shed on the street front and the back of the lot open. Along Passaic Avenue are an old school marked as still in use, a church, stores near Main, a carpenter's shop and a grain store. St. Paul's Episcopal Church stands at the corner of Main and Bowers Lane. The lots on both sides of North Summit Avenue are drawn as a dense run of narrow strips, and a foundry and its sheds stand near Florham Road. At the lower right, beside Hedges Avenue, a block of greenhouses with a potting house stands at the east end. South of Hedges Avenue the block 35 is largely unbuilt, with Munn Avenue drawn as not opened, and Minton Avenue and the Morris County Traction Company right of way cross Main near the bottom left. The Passaic River forms the lower edge, with the borough line and Essex County lettered beside it. Hydrants and water pipes of 4, 6 and 8 inches are marked. The adjoining sheets are numbered 1, 6, 8 and 10 and the title and scale bar are in the margins.
notes: Canvas sheet-8 is printed sheet 9.
Passaic Avenue is North Passaic Avenue in OpenStreetMap. Munn Avenue is drawn as not opened and is not in today's street network; Florham Road is not in the network under that name.

Weston Avenue is drawn about 33 to 35 ft wide against 50 ft in the parcels; its junctions were kept, with residuals up to 4.5 m (Hedges Avenue / Weston Avenue) and Main Street / North Hillside Avenue at 4.3 m.
The Morris County Traction Co. right of way is lettered at the lower left.
Printed sheet 9, 100 ft. North-east: Passaic Avenue, Summit Avenue, Hedges and Weston Avenues. Weston Avenue drawn about 34 ft wide.

sheet-9-1.description: The main part of sheet 10 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the eastern end of the borough between Main Street at the top and the Passaic River, which bends around the bottom and right of the sheet and forms the boundary with the City of Summit and Essex County. Main Street is built up with frame dwellings, an auto and paint shop and the Chatham Hotel on its north side; at its east end it crosses the outlet of a pond on a small bridge and continues across the river as the Morris and Essex Turnpike. Beside the pond stand the Chatham Laundry Company's wet wash laundry, with its boiler room and an auto house drawn from plans, and a dance hall on the pond's east shore. Minton Avenue runs south from Main Street past a few dwellings to Myrtle Avenue, Fern Avenue and Vine, and Summit Avenue appears at the lower left where it crosses the river on a bridge. Most of the sheet is open land in large blocks numbered 125, 126 and 127, crossed from top to bottom by the right of way of the Morris County Traction Company. Munn Avenue is shown leaving Main Street at the top. Hydrants, water pipes and house numbers are marked on the built-up streets, and the borough line follows the river. A separately framed part at the upper left of the sheet, divided off by a heavy line, shows the Watchung Avenue bridge and is described on its own.
notes: The north arrow points to magnetic north; the fitted rotation puts true north about 7.5 degrees clockwise of the top of the sheet.
The Morris County Traction Company right of way, the pond and the laundry are gone; Main Street east of Minton Avenue is now part of NJ 124.
Munn Avenue is not in today's street network under that name.
Few junctions survive on this part (Main Street, Minton Avenue, Myrtle, Fern and Vine, Summit Avenue), most along Minton Avenue, so its fit is weak.

Printed sheet 10, 100 ft. East end along Main Street to the Passaic River (Summit line); open land in the river bend. Part 1 main map (weak, points mostly along Minton Avenue); part 2 framed inset of the Watchung Avenue bridge, anchored on one hand-picked point.

sheet-9-2.description: A separately framed part at the upper left of sheet 10 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, divided from the main map by a heavy line and drawn at 100 feet to an inch. It shows Watchung Avenue, 50 feet wide, running down to the Passaic River and crossing it on a bridge to the City of Summit, with the city line drawn through the river. Two frame dwellings stand between Watchung Avenue and the river bank, and the outline of a block belonging to sheet 5 is repeated at the upper left. A small backwater of the river curves under the west end of the bridge. The rest of the frame is blank paper, with the note directing the reader to the map of Summit along the heavy dividing line. Sheet numbers 5, 6 and 11 mark the neighbouring sheets.
notes: Placed from one hand-picked point, the middle of the Watchung Avenue bridge (the OpenStreetMap bridge way's midpoint), with the scale and rotation of the atlas's other 100 ft sheets; low confidence.
The drawn bridge is about 51 m long against 39 m for the modern bridge way.

Printed sheet 10, 100 ft. East end along Main Street to the Passaic River (Summit line); open land in the river bend. Part 1 main map (weak, points mostly along Minton Avenue); part 2 framed inset of the Watchung Avenue bridge, anchored on one hand-picked point.

sheet-10.description: Printed sheet 11 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, drawn at 100 feet to an inch, covers the south-eastern corner of the borough between Hillside Avenue on the west and the Passaic River on the east. The sheet is turned on the page, so Watchung Avenue runs across the top from left to right to the river bridge, and River Road runs down the right-hand side beside the tracks of the Delaware, Lackawanna and Western Railroad. At the top left, blocks 44 and 45 lie between Hillside Avenue, Girard Avenue and Watchung Avenue, with scattered frame dwellings, coops and sheds; La Fayette Place and Clifton Place enter from the left edge. The railroad runs north to south through the middle of the sheet, and beside it Jas. Wagner's greenhouses and a Standard Oil station with its tanks, a paint shop and carpenter shop stand on the east side. The large block 144 east of River Road has a few dwellings and open fields running to the Passaic River, which bounds the east side with the City of Summit beyond it. Perrin and an unnamed lane cross River Road in the lower right, with blocks 154 and 155. South of Willow, the blocks 150, 151, 152 and 153 are cut into narrow lots with some dwellings, a greenhouse and a garage, with Chestnut and Maple Street and Lackawanna Avenue curving down towards River Road at the bottom. The railroad crosses the river at the bottom edge. Hydrants and water pipes of 4 and 6 inches are marked. Sheets 5, 10 and 12 adjoin on the margins.
notes: Canvas sheet-10 is printed sheet 11.
Clifton Place and Lackawanna Avenue are not in today's street network. Willow, Chestnut, Maple and Perrin are Willow Street, Chestnut Street, Maple Street and Perrin Street in OpenStreetMap.

Perrin / River Road is 7.6 m from the fit of the other junctions and was left out; River Road on the east side of the railroad is placed from one junction at Watchung Avenue and checks against the modern line to about 3 to 5 m.
Jas. Wagner's greenhouses and a Standard Oil station are on the sheet; the Watchung Avenue bridge and the river bridge at the bottom edge adjoin sheets 10 and 12.
La Fayftte Place is printed with that misspelling ("LA FAYFTTE PL."); it is Lafayette Place today.
Printed sheet 11, 100 ft. South-east: Hillside Avenue, River Road, Watchung Avenue, Willow and Chestnut Streets, railroad, Passaic River. Perrin Street / River Road left out (7.6 m).

sheet-12-1.description: The main part of sheet 12 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas is drawn at 200 feet to an inch, half the scale of the other sheets, and covers the thinly built southern end of the borough. The sheet is turned so that north points to the upper left. It runs from Lafayette Avenue and Watchung Avenue at the upper left, where the borough line comes in from Chatham Township, across Washington Avenue, Delwood Avenue, Highland Avenue, Fairmount Avenue and Hillside Avenue to River Road and the Passaic River, the boundary with the City of Summit, at the right. Chandler Road, Fairview Avenue, Greenwood Avenue and Longwood Avenue cross these streets, and Longwood Avenue and a dash-dot line mark the borough line along the bottom, with Chatham Township beyond. Most blocks (133, 139 to 141, 145 to 149, 153, 156 to 162) are laid out in house lots with only scattered dwellings, many of them stuccoed or of hollow tile, and a water works stand pipe stands near Longwood Avenue. At the upper right the denser blocks around Edgehill Avenue, Charles Place, Lafayette Place and Clifton Place are built with dwellings and auto houses, and beside Hillside Avenue are the machine shop and packing and labelling buildings of the Vapo-Cresolene Manufacturing Company. Willow Street, Chestnut Street and Maple Street leave Hillside Avenue towards sheet 11, Ascension Place meets Fairmount Avenue at the top, and Amherst runs between Chandler Road and Fairview Avenue. A separately framed part at the lower left, divided off by a heavy line, is described on its own.
notes: Drawn at 200 ft to an inch; the other sheets are at 100 ft.
Delwood Avenue is spelled Dellwood Avenue today; Amherst is Amherst Road.
Ascension Place and Clifton Place are not in today's street network.
The drawn Orchard Road is about 163 m from Watchung Avenue along Lafayette Avenue, against 130 m between the modern junctions.

Junctions left out of the fit as 8 to 11 m off: Edgehill Avenue / Lafayette Place, Chandler Road / Washington Avenue, Hillside Avenue / Willow Street; Lafayette Avenue / Watchung Avenue was hand-picked.
The Vapo-Cresolene Manufacturing Company works stands beside Hillside Avenue.

Printed sheet 12, 200 ft (scan of another copy). South: Washington, Fairmount, Hillside, Highland, Delwood, Greenwood, Fairview, Longwood Avenues, Chandler Road, River Road; a separately boxed part at lower left (Lafayette Avenue, Orchard Road, Watchung Avenue). Part 2 (lower left) anchored on one hand-picked point at Lafayette / Watchung; drawn spacing along Lafayette disagrees with modern junctions.

sheet-12-2.description: A separately framed part at the lower left of sheet 12 of the November 1921 Chatham atlas, divided from the main map by a heavy line and drawn at the same 200 feet to an inch. It shows Lafayette Avenue, 50 feet wide, running from its junction with Chatham Street, marked by a hydrant, past Orchard Road to Watchung Avenue at the bottom edge, and the open land of block 116 to the west of it. Two dash-dot lines cross the block: one lettered A and B, and the borough line, with Chatham Township beyond it to the south-west. No buildings are drawn. The sheet numbers 2 and 3 mark the neighbouring sheets, and the main map's sheet 12 continues along Watchung Avenue.
notes: Placed from one hand-picked point, Lafayette Avenue / Watchung Avenue at the bottom edge, with the scale and rotation of sheet 12's main part; low confidence.

Along Lafayette Avenue the drawn junctions do not match the modern spacing: Chatham Street to Watchung Avenue is about 318 m on the sheet against 292 m today, and Orchard Road sits about 151 m from Chatham Street against 162 m.

Printed sheet 12, 200 ft (scan of another copy). South: Washington, Fairmount, Hillside, Highland, Delwood, Greenwood, Fairview, Longwood Avenues, Chandler Road, River Road; a separately boxed part at lower left (Lafayette Avenue, Orchard Road, Watchung Avenue). Part 2 (lower left) anchored on one hand-picked point at Lafayette / Watchung; drawn spacing along Lafayette disagrees with modern junctions.
